title: Macrophage ILF3 promotes abdominal aortic aneurysm by inducing inflammatory imbalance in male mice

predicted_errors.error_location: Results section describing ILF3^M-Tg and ILF3^M-KO mouse models
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper describes the macrophage ILF3 conditional overexpression mice as 'ILF3^flox/floxLysMCre^+' (referred to as ILF3^M–Tg) and later describes the macrophage-ILF3 knockout mice using the exact same genotype notation 'ILF3^flox/floxLysMCre^+' (referred to as ILF3^M–KO). These are described as two functionally opposite mouse models (one for gain-of-function overexpression, one for loss-of-function knockout), yet they are assigned identical genetic notation without any distinguishing allele designation (e.g., a stop-cassette transgene vs. a floxed endogenous exon). This is internally inconsistent since the same genotype symbol cannot logically represent both an overexpression construct and a knockout construct.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results text on scRNA-seq analysis vs. Figure 1J caption
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The main text states: 'we utilized Seurat for analyzing human single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE166676)... Through UMAP and canonical markers, we classified cells into seven types (Supplementary Figs. 1D, E).' However, the Figure 1 caption for panel J states: 'ILF3⁺ macrophages from human AAA and non-aneurysmal samples were projected onto the t-SNE plot.' This is inconsistent — the methodology explicitly describes UMAP for dimensionality reduction/clustering, but the figure caption describes a t-SNE plot for the same dataset, without any explanation for switching embedding methods.

predicted_errors.error_location: Mechanistic results paragraph describing EMSA findings (preceding Figure 5K, L description)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states: 'EMSA showed decreased NF-κB DNA binding and elevated Nrf2-ARE DNA binding in ILF3-deficient macrophages, in particular increased Nrf2 binding to the ARE sequence of key inflammatory genes (e.g., MCP1...).' This conflates two distinct regulatory elements/pathways: MCP-1 (CCL2) is a classic NF-κB-responsive pro-inflammatory chemokine gene, not an antioxidant-response-element (ARE)-regulated Nrf2 target gene. Describing Nrf2 as binding an 'ARE sequence' of an inflammatory gene like MCP1 is biologically implausible as commonly characterized in the literature and represents a mischaracterization of the molecular mechanism.
